Silk Road Expeditions

Han-Xiongnu Wars
Likes civilizations that clear out barbarian outposts. Dislikes warmongers with emphasis of cavalry units.
Liu Che is impressed by your efforts to cleanse the barbarians’ presence.
(You clear out barbarian outposts.)
Liu Che is dismayed by your cavalry units and warmongering behavior.
(You are a warmonger who emphasizes cavalry units.)

May your reign be eternal, ambitious Emperor of the Great Han. The lands beyond the Great Wall lie multitudes of opportunities and threats, and the Chinese people look to your visionary. Send the ambassadors and caravans to establish a network of trade routes that the world has never seen before, and crush those ignorant enough to stand in your way.
I am the Son of Heaven, the Emperor of the Great Han. Declare your name and describe your tribes. The Grand Historian will keep the record for good.
Our bustling marketplaces are open to all. You may come to pay a visit.
Fine.
You may write poems about the magnificence of Weiyang Palace. I will let my scholars do the same for your court.
What do you bring to my court today? Gifts of tribute? A trade agreement?
Choose your words wisely.
Your delegation may choose a mansion on the Gao Street to stay, provided they keep their manners like the other foreigners.
Gao Street has nowhere for your delegation to stay now.
The trade delegation of the Great Han is reaching your lands. The leader is carrying a red jie-staff, with gifts of lacquerware, jadeware, bronzeware and our finest silk.
The Emperor of the Great Han bestow upon your people the permission to pass the Middle Kingdom.
Our border must be kept secure and shut.
The people of the Middle Kingdom seek opportunities in lands beyond the Great Wall. Allow my loyal servants to pass your realm peacefully.
Your offer suits my interests.
There is a long way to go before you could even draw parallel between your clans to the Great Han.
Your people are allowed to call themselves friends of the Great Han, How about that?
Your prudence is remarkable.
I overestimated your abilities to comprehend the situation.
I seek common allies to expand our trade network and keep the people living on the borders safe. Are you wise enough to claim this opportunity?
Those vermins must be wiped out before they spawn too many. I appreciate your swift resolution.
Fine horses are gifts from the Heaven for wise leaders, not for bloodthirsty marauders.
The captivating scenery of the Great Han is well known in all four corners of the world, but your troops stay too close. Stay back. Your troops may enjoy the scenery from a distance.
Our sentinels have lit brazen to warn your military presence. Remove them immediately, or my generals will take the task.
The guards of our caravans bear no ill intentions, but I guess they look too intimidating in your eyes. Fine, they will stay back from your lands.
Your request is accepted. For now.
You are more cautious than I expected. Prepare for war!
Those lands are reserved for Tuntian settlements. Watch your manners next time.
Those lands are reserved for Tuntian settlements. Your insolent actions could bear grave consequences.
Fine. The people of the Great Han can always find better lands to settle.
Your request is accepted. For now.
All lands under the Heaven belong to the Great Han. Despite your humble request, the Tuntian plan cannot be disrupted.
All lands under the Heaven belong to the Great Han. The Tuntian plan will not be disrupted by your insolent claims.
I am interested in this trade agreement.
On behalf of my people, I must agree.
Negotiation is an art. Mutual benefits must be sought.
Are you attempting to amuse me? Try harder next time.
Another tribe failed to recognize the splendor of the Great Han. How pathetic.
You are an avaricious barbarian. Beneath your human frame lies the fetid heart of a foul beast. (Denounces You)
You dare to offend the mighty Han? Your head would look good when hanged from the North Gate.
You stand in the way of the mighty Han. Destruction is your only fate!
Good. This war has gone too long.
No. You bandits can still fight, and so do I!
When the soldiers fight, the peasants suffer. It is time to put down our arms.
All glories and failures under the Heaven are my properties! The people have no part in this.

Liu Che
Emperor of the Han Dynasty
An unruly horse may run a thousand li, and a teased man may achieve great successes. The point is who harness them.
Liu Che seeks to expand the influence of China by trade, and crush the obstacles on his way by might.

In the early game, train Builders and use their charges to accelerate Ancient and Classical wonders, while your Marquis(es) of Bowang use their outstanding [ICON_Strength] Combat Strength and sight to search for city-states, other civilizations and lands with resources. Each original [ICON_Capital] Capital you control provides +1 Influence Point per turn, helping you earn Envoys and cultivate city-state relationships. Your land units also fight with +5 [ICON_Strength] Combat Strength outside home territory, allowing you to protect your interests or crush your opponents. Conquest of foreign [ICON_Capital] Capitals adds more original capitals to your empire, further increasing your Influence Points and supporting an ever-stronger army. As wonder building, diplomacy and military power reinforce each other, Liu Che’s dominance is unshakable.

The largest ethnic group of China (and the world), Han Chinese, is named after the prominent Han Dynasty; and the Han Dynasty’s preeminence is commonly attributed to the reign of the seventh Emperor, Liu Che, also known as Emperor Wu (“Martial”) of Han. Under his leadership, the Empire’s border stretched from Korean peninsula to Fergana valley, and the Chinese influence even more.

In 141 BC, Liu Che was born as the eleventh son of the Emperor Han Jingdi with an auspicious omen, and grew with less lucky brothers. Liu Che replaced his eldest brother as the crown prince, and subsequently ascended to the throne in his teens.

At that time, the noble lords were unruly enough to rebel against the Emperors time by time. Even worse, the borders of the Empire were under the threats of the Xiongnu, a confederation of nomads and raiders. The former Han Emperors could only maintain wavering peace by routinely appeasing the Xiongnu leaders with luxuries and princesses, and focused on economic recovery instead. This stalemate of humiliation did not suit the new Emperor’s interests. Inheriting the enormous wealth and grains from his grandfather’s and his father’s reign, Liu Che sought a change, a complete change.

Liu Che consolidated his power via promotion of talented commoners, and encouraged the feudal lords to "show grace" by passing on their territory to not only a single heir, but divided among all sons. Only few at that time could tell his true intentions: by doing so, the Emperor weakened the power of each individual feudal lords without direct clash. More importantly, he endorsed Confucianism as the sole imperial doctrine while shunning all other philosophies as "unorthodox". The Confucian concepts of loyalty and filial piety solidified national harmony – and imperial power, of course. Liu Che also performed many economic reforms to have an iron grip of the economy to serve his agenda.

The multitudes of internal reforms did not distract Liu Che from looking beyond the Great Wall. After the failed attempts of ambushing the Xiongnu cavalrymen at the city of Mayi, the Emperor ordered expeditions into the northern steppe. Imperial envoys like Zhan Qian and Su Wu were tasked to collect information of lands beyond the Great Wall, and seek allies of other steppe nations against the Xiongnu raiders. Military commanders like Li Guang, Wei Qing and Huo Qubing led elite forces to drive away the Xiongnu. Many victories were accomplished, the expedition force even performed a ritual at Khentii Mountains, the holy site of the Xiongnu tribes. The forces of territorial expansion were unstoppable, and many other kingdoms were conquered or subdued by the Han forces.

Liu Che ordered the establishment of a series of garrisons on the newly acquired territories. Soldiers and farmers were encouraged to settle in these places to keep the land rich and safe. With the nomad raiders mostly neutralized, merchants from China and all neighboring nations rushed to this region, later known as the Silk Road, the bridge that connected the East and the West to exchange silk, porcelain, tea leaves and innovative ideas.

Even the finest stallion would eventually grow old. The visionary of Liu Che was eventually clouded by arrogance, superstition and old age, and committed a whole bunch of mistakes in his late reign. Unnecessary expenditures were made, and honest officials were tortured. (For example, the Grand Historian Sima Qian was castrated.) Eventually, he misjudged the crown prince for performing witchcraft and plotting rebellions, eventually leading to the latter’s suicide. In his final years, Liu Che reflected upon the disastrous consequences of extended warfare and his own policy mistakes, declared an imperial edict of public apology (he was the first one to do so), and allowed the economy to recover. The regretful Emperor died in 87 BC, leaving behind an Empire with roughly doubled territories, a set of political philosophy adopted by the future generations, and a nation who fear the external threats no more.

Marquis of Bowang
Chinese unique Ancient Era unit that replaces the Scout, when Liu Che is their leader. Stronger and greater sight than the Scout that it replaces.
+2 Sight.
+2 Sight.
Exceptional Mobility
The Marquis of Bowang has exceptional mobility.

Around the time of the Han-Xiongnu Wars, the imperial envoys of Han Empire were not merely diplomats. They needed outstanding survival skills plus a huge amount of luck, or they would be captured by the Xiongnu raiders and disappeared in the lands outside the Great Wall. The first successful official was Zhang Qian. Twice captured and twice escaped, he brought back precious first-hand information to Chang’an, about the steppe, the Xiongnu and other Central Asian kingdoms. For his achievement, Liu Che granted Zhang Qian the title of palace consellor and later, the Marquis of Bowang (“Bowang” meaning “broad vision”). Zhang Qian was considered the traiblazer of diplomatic and commercial exchange between the East and the West, and the later Han envoys were called “Marquis of Bowang” as the legacy of trust.
